numbers.note: The Singapore 2026 column uses the latest published figures where marked ✓ (Population in Brief 2026, SingStat, PUB, the national climate study V3). Rows marked ‡ are from the drafting team's memory and need a source check before any publication. The four 2065 columns are not forecasts. They are the drafting team's illustrative reading of each scenario's internal logic, offered to be challenged. Rows in the climate block are set by physics, not governance, and barely differ across worlds.

extrapolated: A hotter, wetter island: the national climate study (V3) projects sea-level rise of up to 1.15 m by 2100, and roughly 30% of the land lies less than 5 m above sea level.
A super-aged society: 21.4% of citizens were 65 or older in 2026, heading past one in four by 2035, with fertility at 0.87.
The water clock: the 1962 Johor water agreement ends in 2061, and the plan is for NEWater and desalination to meet up to 85% of demand by 2060.
A small, open labour market: about 1.98 million of the 6.21 million people living in Singapore are non-residents.
AI and automation reshaping which jobs exist, and who holds them.
yours: What a social compact means in 2065: who owns, who decides, who pays.
Whether the hub stays indispensable, and what it sells if it does not.
The relationships with Malaysia, Indonesia, China, the US, India and the Gulf.
The place of the non-resident workforce.
The person on the street: the layer we most want you to test.

forces.p: Heat and sea level arrive whoever governs, so the climate record is the same in all four 2065s. What differs is adaptive capacity: A builds the sea wall with citizens' consent; B builds it slowly and shares the cost by rule; C builds it fast and asks few questions; D builds it in pieces, behind a security fence.

Fewer than two working citizens support each citizen aged 65 or over by 2065 in every world. The question is who pays and who is asked: a care guarantee in A, a service obligation in B, a market in C, a quota in D.

forces.h: AI and the future of work
forces.p: AI absorbs routine cognitive work everywhere. In A it funds retraining wages, in B it is rationed towards resilience, in C its gains accrue to capital and mobile talent, and in D it is turned inward as a tool of control.

forcesTitle: Three forces above the four futures

matrixRead.tension: Can a broad, argumentative compact keep building capacity faster than ageing and the sea erode it?
matrixRead.watch: A standing assembly with a real budget line; citizen income tracking GDP; orderly Johor negotiations.

matrixRead.tension: The hub shrinks but the people hold together: does cohesion outrun decline?
matrixRead.watch: Published ration and reserve rules; regional resource pacts; non-residents inside the burden-sharing.

matrixRead.tension: Stability and speed are bought by narrowing who is asked, while the citizen core slips from owner to tenant.
matrixRead.watch: Citizen share of senior jobs; lease-end policy; funding for civil society; share of citizens working for global employers.

matrixRead.tension: Insecurity becomes the rationale for control, and control forecloses adaptation.
matrixRead.watch: Emergency orders renewed as routine; emigration of citizens aged 25 to 40; non-resident quotas cut by decree.

dynamics: The two axes are not independent. A fragmenting world pushes the system towards securitised, centralised control, which narrows the compact. Equally, a narrow compact leaves a state with less consent and less adaptive capacity just when the world turns harder, which makes fragmentation more costly. The benign task is to hold the top left. The danger is a diagonal drift towards the bottom right, where each axis worsens the other. For each scenario participants build, name the quadrant it starts in, the direction it is drifting, and the one or two choices that would move it, in either direction.

x.title: The world around Singapore
x.def: Whether trade, capital, data and sea lanes stay open and rules-based, or split into rival blocs, sanction regimes and contested chokepoints.

y.title: Breadth of the social compact
y.def: How widely the gains, the risks and the say in national decisions are shared among citizens: median income against GDP, who owns the home and the wealth, and how much of the budget and the rules citizens can shape.

axes.why: A city-state with no hinterland lives or dies on two things: whether the world still needs the hub, and whether its own people stay with it while it adapts. The first is largely outside Singapore's control. The second is largely inside it. Crossing them gives four archetypes.
